---
title: "Stationary Does Not Mean Convergent"
description: "A two-state Markov chain can oscillate around its unique stationary distribution. Averaging its distributions restores convergence."
categories: ["Probability", "Linear Algebra"]
---

## A Chain That Keeps Switching

Start in state 1. At each step, switch to the other state. The chain is in state 1 at even times and state 2 at odd times. Its distribution alternates between $(1,0)^\top$ and $(0,1)^\top$.

Now start with equal chances of being in the two states. Switching leaves those chances equal. In fact, the uniform distribution is the only one left unchanged by a swap. The same chain has a unique stationary distribution and a starting distribution that never converges to it.

## Stationarity and Limits

We write distributions as column vectors. In a transition matrix $P$, the entry $P_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$ in one step. Its entries are nonnegative, and each column sums to one. A matrix with these properties is **column-stochastic**.

If the same transition rule is used at every step, then $x_{k+1}=Px_k$, where $x_k$ is the distribution at time $k$. A distribution $\pi$ is **stationary** if $P\pi=\pi$. Once the chain has distribution $\pi$, every later distribution is also $\pi$.

If $x_k$ converges to a distribution $x$, we can pass to the limit in $x_{k+1}=Px_k$ to get $x=Px$. Thus any limit must be stationary. The swapping example shows why stationarity alone gives no assurance that a limit exists.

## Switching with Probability $t$

Suppose the chain switches with probability $t$ and stays where it is with probability $1-t$. Its matrix is

$$
P_t=\begin{pmatrix}1-t&t\\t&1-t\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 0\le t\le1.
$$

Let $\pi=(1/2,1/2)^\top$ and $w=(1,-1)^\top$. Direct multiplication gives $P_t\pi=\pi$ and $P_tw=(1-2t)w$. If $x_0=(p,1-p)^\top$, then $x_0=\pi+(p-1/2)w$. For $k\ge1$,

$$
x_k=\pi+(p-1/2)(1-2t)^k w.
$$

The coefficient of $w$ measures the imbalance between the states. The factor $1-2t$ determines what happens to it:

- At $t=0$, the chain never moves. Every distribution is stationary.
- For $0<t<1/2$, the imbalance decays without changing sign.
- At $t=1/2$, the imbalance is zero after one step.
- For $1/2<t<1$, the imbalance flips sign at every step and decays in size.
- At $t=1$, the imbalance flips sign at every step and keeps its size. Only the starting distribution $\pi$ gives a convergent sequence.

For every $t>0$, stationarity requires the imbalance to be zero. Thus $\pi$ is unique throughout this range, including the swapping case. The value $t=1/4$ is the smaller transition matrix in [What Changes When You Swap the Factors?](../linear-algebra/swapping-matrix-factors.qmd).

## Averaging the Distributions

For the swap, the mean of the first two distributions is $\pi$, no matter where the chain starts. The same holds for the mean of the first $N$ distributions whenever $N$ is even. If $N$ is odd, one unmatched term has weight $1/N$, which tends to zero.

This idea applies to any finite Markov chain with a unique stationary distribution. Define the average of the first $N$ distribution vectors by

$$
\bar x_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x_k.
$$

Applying $P$ shifts the sum by one step. Subtracting the original sum cancels all but the endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\bar x_N-\bar x_N
  &=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(x_{k+1}-x_k)\\
  &=\frac{x_N-x_0}{N}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Every coordinate of a distribution lies between zero and one. Therefore the last expression tends to zero.

All the averages lie in the **probability simplex**, the set of nonnegative vectors whose coordinates sum to one. For finitely many states this set is closed and bounded, hence compact. Every subsequence of the averages has a further subsequence converging to some probability vector $y$. Along that subsequence, the identity above gives $Py=y$. By uniqueness, $y=\pi$.

It follows that $\bar x_N\to\pi$. If the averages failed to converge to $\pi$, some subsequence would stay a positive distance away from it. Compactness would give that subsequence a limit different from $\pi$, contradicting uniqueness.
